ASSUME NoCar \notin Cars

VARIABLES queued, manifest, logged, token, onAir

TypeOK ==
  /\ queued \subseteq Calls
  /\ manifest \in [Cars -> SUBSET Calls]
  /\ logged \subseteq Calls
  /\ token \in Cars \cup {NoCar}
  /\ onAir \subseteq Cars

OnSomeManifest == UNION {manifest[c] : c \in Cars}

CallsConserved ==
  /\ queued \cup OnSomeManifest \cup logged = Calls
  /\ queued \cap logged = {}
  /\ queued \cap OnSomeManifest = {}
  /\ logged \cap OnSomeManifest = {}
  /\ \A a, b \in Cars : a # b => manifest[a] \cap manifest[b] = {}

Init ==
  /\ queued = Calls
  /\ manifest = [c \in Cars |-> {}]
  /\ logged = {}
  /\ token \in Cars
  /\ onAir = {}

ReleaseToken(c) ==
  /\ token = c
  /\ \E d \in Cars \ {c} : onAir' = onAir \cup {d}
  /\ token' = NoCar
  /\ UNCHANGED <<queued, manifest, logged>>

DeliverGrant(d) ==
  /\ token = NoCar
  /\ d \in onAir
  /\ onAir' = onAir \ {d}
  /\ token' = d
  /\ UNCHANGED <<queued, manifest, logged>>

TakeCall(c, k) ==
  /\ token = c
  /\ k \in queued
  /\ queued' = queued \ {k}
  /\ manifest' = [manifest EXCEPT ![c] = @ \cup {k}]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<logged, token, onAir>>

CompleteCall(c, k) ==
  /\ k \in manifest[c]
  /\ manifest' = [manifest EXCEPT ![c] = @ \ {k}]
  /\ logged' = logged \cup {k}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<queued, token, onAir>>

PushBack(c, k) ==
  /\ token = c
  /\ k \in manifest[c]
  /\ manifest' = [manifest EXCEPT ![c] = @ \ {k}]
  /\ queued' = queued \cup {k}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<logged, token, onAir>>

Next ==
  \E c \in Cars :
    \/ ReleaseToken(c)
    \/ DeliverGrant(c)
    \/ \E k \in Calls : TakeCall(c, k) \/ CompleteCall(c, k) \/ PushBack(c, k)

TokenMoves == \E c \in Cars : ReleaseToken(c) \/ DeliverGrant(c)

SomeComplete == \E c \in Cars, k \in Calls : CompleteCall(c, k)

  /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ WF_vars(TokenMoves)
  /\ SF_vars(SomeTake)
  /\ SF_vars(SomeComplete)

CONSTANTS
    Cars = {ecA, ecB}
    Calls = {hcA, hcB}
    NoCar = noCar
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT CallsConserved
PROPERTY EveryWaitingCallIsLogged
nl:
A skyscraper elevator bank runs its cars off a single dispatch token that circulates around a ring. Only the car currently holding the token is allowed to reach into the building-wide hall-call queue: it may take a waiting hall call for itself, or hand a call it had previously taken back to the queue when it realises it cannot reach that floor on its present run. A car does not need the token to finish work it already owns -- once a call is on a car's own manifest, that car can drive to the floor, open the doors and mark the call complete at any time.

The token is passed by radio rather than by wire, and the radio layer reorders traffic. When the holder gives up the token it names a successor and the grant goes out onto the air; the token is considered to be nowhere at all until some outstanding grant is actually picked up by the car it names. Because grants can sit on the air and overtake one another, the car that finally receives the token need not be the one the most recent holder named, and a grant issued early can be the one that lands last.

Every hall call in the building is one of exactly three things at any instant: still waiting in the shared queue, sitting on the manifest of exactly one car, or completed and logged. Calls are never invented by the dispatcher and never quietly dropped when a car abandons them -- an abandoned call goes back to the shared queue rather than disappearing. The actions of the system are: the token holder releasing the token and putting a grant on the air, an outstanding grant being delivered to the car it names, the token holder taking a waiting call onto its manifest, any car completing a call on its manifest, and the token holder pushing one of its own manifest entries back into the shared queue.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The set of hall calls is conserved as a partition -- every call is waiting, or on exactly one car's manifest, or completed, and never in two of those places at once.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every hall call that is waiting in the shared queue is eventually completed and logged.

CONSTANTS Boxes, PickFleet, RepFleet, PoolCap, MaxTerm, NoBox

       /\ PickFleet # RepFleet
       /\ PoolCap \in Nat /\ MaxTerm \in Nat

VARIABLES coord, term, docked, permits, dead

vars == <<coord, term, docked, permits, dead>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ coord \in [Fleets -> Boxes \cup {NoBox}]
  /\ term \in [Fleets -> 0 .. MaxTerm]
  /\ docked \in [Fleets -> 0 .. PoolCap]
  /\ permits \in [Fleets -> 0 .. PoolCap]
  /\ dead \subseteq Boxes

Committed ==
  docked[PickFleet] + permits[PickFleet] + docked[RepFleet] + permits[RepFleet]

PoolNeverOversubscribed == Committed <= PoolCap

Init ==
  /\ coord = [f \in Fleets |-> NoBox]
  /\ term = [f \in Fleets |-> 0]
  /\ docked = [f \in Fleets |-> 0]
  /\ permits = [f \in Fleets |-> 0]
  /\ dead = {}

Elect(f, b) ==
  /\ coord[f] = NoBox
  /\ b \notin dead
  /\ b \notin {coord[g] : g \in Fleets}
  /\ coord' = [coord EXCEPT ![f] = b]
  /\ term' = [term EXCEPT ![f] = IF @ < MaxTerm THEN @ + 1 ELSE @]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<docked, permits, dead>>

CoordCrashes(f) ==
  /\ coord[f] # NoBox
  /\ dead' = dead \cup {coord[f]}
  /\ coord' = [coord EXCEPT ![f] = NoBox]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<term, docked, permits>>

IssuePermit(f) ==
  /\ coord[f] # NoBox
  /\ Committed < PoolCap
  /\ permits' = [permits EXCEPT ![f] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coord, term, docked, dead>>

Redeem(f) ==
  /\ permits[f] > 0
  /\ permits' = [permits EXCEPT ![f] = @ - 1]
  /\ docked' = [docked EXCEPT ![f] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coord, term, dead>>

LeaveDock(f) ==
  /\ docked[f] > 0
  /\ docked' = [docked EXCEPT ![f] = @ - 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coord, term, permits, dead>>

TimeOutPermit(f) ==
  /\ coord[f] = NoBox
  /\ permits[f] > 0
  /\ permits' = [permits EXCEPT ![f] = @ - 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coord, term, docked, dead>>

SwapInSpare(b) ==
  /\ b \in dead
  /\ dead' = dead \ {b}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<coord, term, docked, permits>>

Next ==
  \/ \E b \in Boxes : SwapInSpare(b)
  \/ \E f \in Fleets :
    \/ \E b \in Boxes : Elect(f, b)
    \/ CoordCrashes(f)
    \/ IssuePermit(f)
    \/ Redeem(f)
    \/ LeaveDock(f)
    \/ TimeOutPermit(f)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

CONSTANTS
    Boxes = {ctlA, ctlB, ctlC}
    PickFleet = pickFleet
    RepFleet = repFleet
    PoolCap = 3
    MaxTerm = 2
    NoBox = noBox
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT PoolNeverOversubscribed
nl:
A warehouse operator runs two independent robot fleets -- a picking fleet and a replenishment fleet -- that were commissioned separately and never talk to each other. What they do share is one bank of charging docks in the basement, sized for a fixed number of robots at a time. Each fleet has its own coordinator, elected from a small set of controller boxes; the coordinator is the only thing in that fleet allowed to hand out a charging permit, and a robot may only roll onto a dock by redeeming a permit it was handed.

Coordinators fail. When one does, its fleet is left without a coordinator until a new controller box wins the election, and the election bumps that fleet's term number so that operators can tell the new coordinator from the old one, up to the highest term the fleet's counter can record. A controller box that has crashed stays out of the running until a technician swaps a spare into its slot, after which that slot is eligible again. The awkward part is the permits: when a coordinator dies, the permits it handed out are still outstanding, and the robots holding them may still roll onto docks. The fleet must not treat those permits as free space. Only while a fleet has no coordinator at all is it safe to time a stale permit out and hand its space back, because in that window nobody is issuing new ones.

Because the two fleets draw on the same dock bank but each only sees its own books, a permit is only ever issued when the whole bank -- robots already docked in either fleet, plus permits outstanding in either fleet -- still has room for one more. The actions of the system are: electing a coordinator for a fleet, a fleet's coordinator crashing silently and leaving the fleet leaderless, a coordinator issuing a charging permit, a robot redeeming a permit and rolling onto a dock, a robot finishing its charge and leaving the dock, a leaderless fleet timing out one of its outstanding permits, and a technician swapping a spare box into a crashed slot.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of robots docked in the two fleets plus the number of permits still outstanding in the two fleets never exceeds the size of the shared dock bank.

       /\ MaxEpoch \in Nat

VARIABLES epoch, driver, caughtUp, holding, dead

vars == <<epoch, driver, caughtUp, holding, dead>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ epoch \in 0 .. MaxEpoch
  /\ driver \in Controllers \cup {Nobody}
  /\ caughtUp \in [Controllers -> 0 .. MaxEpoch]
  /\ holding \subseteq Controllers
  /\ dead \subseteq Controllers

OnlyNamedDriverHoldsChannel ==
  \A c \in holding : c = driver /\ caughtUp[c] = epoch

Init ==
  /\ epoch = 0
  /\ driver = Nobody
  /\ caughtUp = [c \in Controllers |-> 0]
  /\ holding = {}
  /\ dead = {}

Publish(d) ==
  /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
  /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
  /\ driver' = d
  /\ holding' = {}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<caughtUp, dead>>

CatchUp(c) ==
  /\ caughtUp[c] < epoch
  /\ caughtUp' = [caughtUp EXCEPT ![c] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, driver, holding, dead>>

TakeChannel(c) ==
  /\ c = driver
  /\ c \notin dead
  /\ caughtUp[c] = epoch
  /\ holding = {}
  /\ holding' = {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, driver, caughtUp, dead>>

ReleaseChannel(c) ==
  /\ c \in holding
  /\ c \notin dead
  /\ holding' = holding \ {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, driver, caughtUp, dead>>

Revoke(c) ==
  /\ c \in holding
  /\ c \in dead
  /\ holding' = holding \ {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, driver, caughtUp, dead>>

DieSilently(c) ==
  /\ c \notin dead
  /\ dead' = dead \cup {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, driver, caughtUp, holding>>

PowerCycle(c) ==
  /\ c \in dead
  /\ dead' = dead \ {c}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, driver, caughtUp, holding>>

Next ==
  \/ \E d \in Controllers \cup {Nobody} : Publish(d)
  \/ \E c \in Controllers :
       \/ CatchUp(c) \/ TakeChannel(c) \/ ReleaseChannel(c)
       \/ Revoke(c) \/ DieSilently(c) \/ PowerCycle(c)

SomeRevoke == \E c \in Controllers : Revoke(c)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars /\ SF_vars(SomeRelease) /\ SF_vars(SomeRevoke)

CONSTANTS
    Controllers = {dlA, dlB}
    MaxEpoch = 2
    Nobody = nobodyDrives
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT OnlyNamedDriverHoldsChannel
PROPERTY ChannelIsEventuallyGivenUp
nl:
A smart-home installation has several door-lock controllers wired to one shared unlock channel -- the single low-voltage line that actually throws the deadbolts. Only one controller may be driving that line at a time; two controllers driving it together brown out the bus and leave bolts half-thrown. The hub decides who is allowed to drive it, and it does so by publishing a numbered configuration: each new configuration carries the next epoch number and names exactly one controller as the epoch's designated driver, or names nobody at all while the installer is mid-change.

Controllers learn about new configurations lazily, one epoch at a time, over the same slow mesh that carries battery reports. A controller may only take the channel if it is the controller the current configuration names and it has actually caught up to the current epoch -- a controller that still believes an older configuration is in force must not touch the line, even if it was the driver under that older configuration. Whenever the hub publishes a new configuration it first cuts power to the channel, so nobody is left driving the line across an epoch boundary.

Controllers can also die silently: no error, no last message, just an entry that stops answering. A controller that has died may still be recorded as holding the channel, and the hub cannot wait for it to give the line back politely, so the hub is allowed to revoke the channel from a holder it has marked dead. A healthy holder gives the line back on its own once its bolt sequence finishes. A controller that has died can come back: the installation's nightly power cycle brings a dead unit back onto the mesh, still believing whatever epoch it last learned, and a unit can die again afterwards. The actions of the system are: the hub publishing a new numbered configuration, a controller catching up one epoch, the named driver taking the channel, a healthy holder releasing the channel, the hub revoking the channel from a dead holder, a controller dying silently, and a dead controller coming back on a power cycle.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any controller driving the unlock channel is the controller named by the current configuration and has caught up to the current epoch, so at most one controller ever drives the line.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A controller that has taken the unlock channel eventually stops driving it, whether it releases the line itself or the hub revokes it after the controller dies.

---- MODULE W4Od8m1p4t4 ----
EXTENDS Naturals, FiniteSets

CONSTANTS Fronts, Sections, Students, MaxCap, NoFront

ASSUME /\ NoFront \notin Fronts
       /\ MaxCap \in Nat /\ MaxCap > 0

VARIABLES token, onWire, seat, cap, asked

vars == <<token, onWire, seat, cap, asked>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ token \in Fronts \cup {NoFront}
  /\ onWire \subseteq Fronts
  /\ seat \in [Sections -> [Students -> 0 .. MaxCap]]
  /\ cap \in [Sections -> 1 .. MaxCap]
  /\ asked \subseteq Students

Occupied(s) == {seat[s][st] : st \in {u \in Students : seat[s][u] # 0}}

SeatedWithinCap ==
  \A s \in Sections, st \in Students :
    seat[s][st] # 0 => seat[s][st] <= cap[s]

Init ==
  /\ token \in Fronts
  /\ onWire = {}
  /\ seat = [s \in Sections |-> [st \in Students |-> 0]]
  /\ cap = [s \in Sections |-> MaxCap]
  /\ asked = {}

ReleaseToken(f) ==
  /\ token = f
  /\ \E g \in Fronts \ {f} : onWire' = onWire \cup {g}
  /\ token' = NoFront
  /\ UNCHANGED <<seat, cap, asked>>

PickUpToken(g) ==
  /\ token = NoFront
  /\ g \in onWire
  /\ onWire' = onWire \ {g}
  /\ token' = g
  /\ UNCHANGED <<seat, cap, asked>>

Register(st) ==
  /\ st \notin asked
  /\ asked' = asked \cup {st}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, onWire, seat, cap>>

Seat(f, s, st, n) ==
  /\ token = f
  /\ st \in asked
  /\ seat[s][st] = 0
  /\ n \in 1 .. cap[s]
  /\ n \notin Occupied(s)
  /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![s][st] = n]
  /\ asked' = asked \ {st}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, onWire, cap>>

Drop(s, st) ==
  /\ seat[s][st] # 0
  /\ seat' = [seat EXCEPT ![s][st] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, onWire, cap, asked>>

Resize(f, s, n) ==
  /\ token = f
  /\ n \in 1 .. MaxCap
  /\ \A m \in Occupied(s) : m <= n
  /\ cap' = [cap EXCEPT ![s] = n]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, onWire, seat, asked>>

Next ==
  \/ \E f \in Fronts : ReleaseToken(f) \/ PickUpToken(f)
  \/ \E st \in Students : Register(st)
  \/ \E s \in Sections, st \in Students : Drop(s, st)
  \/ \E f \in Fronts, s \in Sections, st \in Students, n \in 1 .. MaxCap : Seat(f, s, st, n)
  \/ \E f \in Fronts, s \in Sections, n \in 1 .. MaxCap : Resize(f, s, n)

Spec == Init /\ [][Next]_vars

====
nl:
A university's course-registration system runs several registration front ends, and they take turns at the enrolment database by passing a single write token around a ring. A front end may only write an enrolment while it holds the token; when it is done it names a successor and puts the token on the wire, and the successor picks it up. Between the release and the pickup the token is on the wire and nobody may write.

Every section of a course has numbered seats, starting at seat one and running up to the section's current cap. Enrolling a student means writing that student's seat number into the section's roster; a student with no seat number in a section is simply not in it. Two students in the same section are never written into the same seat number, and a student who drops has their seat number cleared, which frees that number for reuse.

The registrar can change a section's cap while registration is running -- opening extra seats when a room is reassigned, or pulling seats back when the fire marshal reduces the room's rating. Raising a cap is always allowed. Lowering it is not free: the registrar may only lower a section's cap to a number that is still at least as large as the highest seat number currently occupied in that section, because there is no mechanism to move a seated student down into a lower-numbered seat. Cap changes go through the token holder like any other write.

The actions of the system are: the token holder releasing the token onto the wire toward a named successor, the named successor picking the token up off the wire, a student submitting a registration request, the token holder seating a requesting student in a free seat number within the section's current cap, a student dropping a section and freeing their seat number, and the token holder changing a section's cap subject to the lowering rule.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every seat number occupied in a section is within that section's current cap, so no student is ever left seated above the cap after a runtime cap change.

EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS EqEngine, DrvEngine, MaxEpoch, MaxBook, Neither

Instances == {EqEngine, DrvEngine}

ASSUME /\ Neither \notin Instances
       /\ EqEngine # DrvEngine
       /\ MaxEpoch \in Nat /\ MaxBook \in Nat

Phases == {"idle", "armed", "printing"}

VARIABLES epoch, authorised, phase, polled, book

vars == <<epoch, authorised, phase, polled, book>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ epoch \in 0 .. MaxEpoch
  /\ authorised \in Instances \cup {Neither}
  /\ phase \in [Instances -> Phases]
  /\ polled \in [Instances -> 0 .. MaxEpoch]
  /\ book \in [Instances -> 0 .. MaxBook]

OnBus == {i \in Instances : phase[i] = "printing"}

PrintBusIsExclusive == OnBus \subseteq {authorised}

Init ==
  /\ epoch = 0
  /\ authorised = Neither
  /\ phase = [i \in Instances |-> "idle"]
  /\ polled = [i \in Instances |-> 0]
  /\ book = [i \in Instances |-> 0]

PublishConfig(a) ==
  /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
  /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
  /\ authorised' = a
  /\ phase' = [i \in Instances |-> IF phase[i] = "printing" THEN "idle" ELSE phase[i]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<polled, book>>

Poll(i) ==
  /\ polled[i] < epoch
  /\ polled' = [polled EXCEPT ![i] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, authorised, phase, book>>

AcceptOrder(i) ==
  /\ book[i] < MaxBook
  /\ book' = [book EXCEPT ![i] = @ + 1]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, authorised, phase, polled>>

Arm(i) ==
  /\ phase[i] = "idle"
  /\ book[i] > 0
  /\ polled[i] = epoch
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![i] = "armed"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, authorised, polled, book>>

TakeBus(i) ==
  /\ phase[i] = "armed"
  /\ i = authorised
  /\ polled[i] = epoch
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![i] = "printing"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, authorised, polled, book>>

FinishPrint(i) ==
  /\ phase[i] = "printing"
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![i] = "idle"]
  /\ book' = [book EXCEPT ![i] = 0]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, authorised, polled>>

StandDown(i) ==
  /\ phase[i] = "armed"
  /\ (i # authorised \/ polled[i] # epoch)
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![i] = "idle"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, authorised, polled, book>>

Next ==
  \/ \E a \in Instances \cup {Neither} : PublishConfig(a)
  \/ \E i \in Instances :
       Poll(i) \/ AcceptOrder(i) \/ Arm(i) \/ TakeBus(i) \/ FinishPrint(i) \/ StandDown(i)

Spec ==
  /\ Init /\ [][Next]_vars
  /\ SF_vars(TakeBus(EqEngine))
  /\ SF_vars(TakeBus(DrvEngine))
  /\ SF_vars(StandDown(EqEngine))
  /\ SF_vars(StandDown(DrvEngine))
  /\ SF_vars(FinishPrint(EqEngine))
  /\ SF_vars(FinishPrint(DrvEngine))

  \A i \in Instances : (phase[i] = "armed") ~> (phase[i] # "armed")

CONSTANTS
    EqEngine = eqEngine
    DrvEngine = drvEngine
    MaxEpoch = 2
    MaxBook = 2
    Neither = neitherEngine
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT PrintBusIsExclusive
PROPERTY ArmedInstancesResolve
nl:
A stock exchange runs its opening auction on two engine instances that were built by different teams and share nothing except the print bus -- the single publication channel on which the official opening price is stamped and sent to the tape. Only one instance may be on the print bus at any moment; a simultaneous stamp would put two opening prices on the tape for the same session, which regulators treat as an incident.

Which instance is entitled to the bus is decided by the exchange's configuration service, which publishes numbered configurations. Each configuration carries the next epoch number and names exactly one instance as that epoch's authorised printer, or names neither while the operations desk is mid-switch. Instances discover new configurations by polling, one epoch at a time, so an instance can be running against a configuration that has already been superseded. An instance that has not caught up to the current epoch is not entitled to anything, and an instance that has caught up but is not the one named is likewise not entitled.

Each instance accumulates unpublished orders in its own book. When an instance has orders waiting and believes it is up to date, it arms itself for a print. An armed instance either goes on to the bus and stamps the price -- which is only possible if it really is the epoch's authorised printer and it really is up to date -- or is stood down, which is what happens when the desk has moved the authorisation elsewhere or the instance turns out to be behind. Finishing a print clears that instance's book and takes it off the bus. A reconfiguration also takes whoever is on the bus off it, so nobody straddles an epoch boundary.

The actions of the system are: the configuration service publishing a new numbered configuration, an instance polling forward one epoch, an instance accepting an order into its book, an instance arming itself for a print, an armed and entitled instance taking the print bus, an instance finishing its print and clearing its book, and an armed instance being stood down.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The set of instances on the print bus is always contained in the set containing just the instance named by the current configuration, so two instances never stamp the tape at once.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: An instance that has armed itself for a print does eventually stop being armed, either by taking the bus and printing or by being stood down.

EXTENDS Naturals

CONSTANTS Attendants, Bays, Revisions, NoAtt, NoBay

ASSUME /\ NoAtt \notin Attendants
       /\ NoBay \notin Bays
       /\ Revisions \in Nat /\ Revisions > 1

VARIABLES line, bayLock, rev, editing, copied, quiet

vars == <<line, bayLock, rev, editing, copied, quiet>>

TypeOK ==
  /\ line \in Attendants \cup {NoAtt}
  /\ bayLock \in [Bays -> Attendants \cup {NoAtt}]
  /\ rev \in [Bays -> 0 .. Revisions - 1]
  /\ editing \in [Attendants -> Bays \cup {NoBay}]
  /\ copied \in [Attendants -> 0 .. Revisions - 1]
  /\ quiet \subseteq Attendants

MidEdit == {a \in Attendants : editing[a] # NoBay}

EditsRestOnCurrentRevision ==
  \A a \in MidEdit :
    /\ line = a
    /\ bayLock[editing[a]] = a
    /\ copied[a] = rev[editing[a]]

Init ==
  /\ line = NoAtt
  /\ bayLock = [b \in Bays |-> NoAtt]
  /\ rev = [b \in Bays |-> 0]
  /\ editing = [a \in Attendants |-> NoBay]
  /\ copied = [a \in Attendants |-> 0]
  /\ quiet = {}

TakeLine(a) ==
  /\ line = NoAtt
  /\ a \notin quiet
  /\ line' = a
  /\ UNCHANGED <<bayLock, rev, editing, copied, quiet>>

TakeBay(a, b) ==
  /\ line = a
  /\ a \notin quiet
  /\ editing[a] = NoBay
  /\ bayLock[b] = NoAtt
  /\ bayLock' = [bayLock EXCEPT ![b] = a]
  /\ editing' = [editing EXCEPT ![a] = b]
  /\ copied' = [copied EXCEPT ![a] = rev[b]]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<line, rev, quiet>>

Commit(a) ==
  /\ a \notin quiet
  /\ editing[a] # NoBay
  /\ copied[a] = rev[editing[a]]
  /\ rev' = [rev EXCEPT ![editing[a]] = (@ + 1) % Revisions]
  /\ bayLock' = [bayLock EXCEPT ![editing[a]] = NoAtt]
  /\ editing' = [editing EXCEPT ![a] = NoBay]
  /\ line' = NoAtt
  /\ UNCHANGED <<copied, quiet>>

DropLine(a) ==
  /\ line = a
  /\ a \notin quiet
  /\ editing[a] = NoBay

CONSTANTS

    Bays = {bayA, bayB}
    Revisions = 2
    NoAtt = noAtt
    NoBay = noBay
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT EditsRestOnCurrentRevision
PROPERTY LineIsEventuallyFreed
nl:
A car-wash conveyor has several wash bays and a handful of attendants working the line. Each bay has a ticket record -- what package the car bought, which extras were added at the arch, whether the wax pass ran. Attendants edit those tickets from a shared terminal, and the shop protects them with two levels of lock taken in a fixed order: first the coarse line lock, which only one attendant can hold at a time and which covers the whole conveyor, then the fine lock on the particular bay whose ticket is being edited. Nobody may touch a bay lock without already holding the line lock, and that ordering is what keeps the shop out of the deadlocks it used to hit when attendants grabbed bays directly.

An edit starts by taking the line lock and then the bay lock, at which point the attendant copies down the bay ticket's current revision number as the basis for its edit. Committing writes the edited ticket back, advances that bay's revision number, drops the bay lock and the line lock together, and lets the next attendant in. A commit is only meaningful if the revision the attendant copied down is still the revision the bay is on -- an edit computed against a revision that has since moved on would silently throw away whatever moved it.

Attendants can walk off. The failure is silent: no handover, no shout down the line, the attendant simply stops and the locks they were holding stay held. The shift supervisor notices eventually, marks the attendant off the line, tears down whatever locks that attendant was holding, throws away their half-finished edit, and puts a replacement on the same station -- so a station that has gone quiet always comes back.

The actions of the system are: an attendant taking the coarse line lock, an attendant who holds the line lock taking a free bay lock and copying down that bay's revision, an attendant committing an edit whose copied revision still matches the bay and dropping both locks, an attendant who holds the line lock but is not mid-edit dropping the line lock, an attendant going quiet without warning, and the supervisor tearing down a quiet attendant's locks and putting a replacement on that station.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every attendant who is mid-edit holds the coarse line lock, holds the fine lock on the bay it is editing, and has copied down exactly the revision that bay is currently on, so no commit can be computed against a revision that has already moved.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: An attendant that has taken the coarse line lock eventually stops holding it, whether by committing, by dropping it, or by the supervisor tearing it down.

CONSTANTS
    BayOne = washBayOne
    BayTwo = washBayTwo
    Units = 3
    MaxTicks = 2
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT BondedStoreReconciles
PROPERTY DayTanksAlwaysDrain
nl:
A car-wash conveyor draws its soap from a bonded store of detergent concentrate. The store is measured in sealed units, and the number of units on the site is fixed for the day: nothing is delivered mid-shift and nothing may be poured away. Units leave the store only on a lease to one of the two wash bays. A lease covers a whole number of units and comes with a countdown; while the countdown is running the units sit in that bay's day tank, still on the books as leased rather than as store stock.

A bay draws down its lease one unit at a time as cars go through, and each unit drawn is logged as consumed. When a lease's countdown reaches zero the lease ends: whatever units are still sitting in that bay's day tank are pumped back to the store and the bay's lease goes to nothing. A bay may only take out a new lease once its previous lease has ended, and a lease can only be granted for units the store actually has.

Bays fail silently. A bay's controller can stop answering with no alarm and no partial-drain report; the units already in its day tank are stranded there and are still leased to that bay, which is exactly why the countdown is on the lease and not on the bay. When the lease expires the stranded units come back to the store whether or not the bay is answering, and a failed bay is eventually power-cycled back onto the line.

The whole point of the bonded store is that the auditor can reconcile at any instant: the units sitting in the store, plus the units leased out to each bay, plus the units logged as consumed, always come to exactly the number of units the site started the day with. The actions of the system are: granting a bay a lease for some units from the store, a bay drawing one leased unit and logging it consumed, a lease's countdown ticking down, a lease expiring and returning its remaining units to the store, a bay failing silently, and a failed bay being power-cycled back onto the line.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The units in the store, plus the units leased to each of the two bays, plus the units logged as consumed always sum to exactly the number of units the site started with.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A bay that is holding leased units eventually holds none, because its lease always runs down and returns whatever is left to the store.

CONSTANTS
    MachOne = vendOne
    MachTwo = vendTwo
    Coins = 3
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT CoinsReconcile
nl:
An operator runs a network of vending machines that all draw change from one bonded coin float held in a central register. The number of coins in the whole system is fixed between route visits: coins move around but none appear and none vanish. A coin is at any instant in exactly one of four places -- sitting in the central float, sitting in a machine's hopper, riding inside a deposit message that a machine has already posted, or already handed to a customer as change.

Machines bank surplus coins by compare-and-swap. A machine takes some coins out of its hopper, notes the value the central register held when it looked, and posts a deposit message carrying both the coins and the noted value. The coins are gone from the hopper the instant the message is posted -- that is what makes them the message's coins and not the hopper's. Messages sit on the operator's slow message bus and the bus reorders them freely, so by the time a message is processed the register may have moved on.

Processing a message is the compare-and-swap. If the register still holds the value the machine noted, the swap takes: the coins in the message are added to the register and the message is retired. If the register has moved on, the swap is refused: the message is retired and its coins go back to the hopper of the machine that posted it, to be tried again later. Either way the coins in a message end up somewhere -- they are never dropped on the floor because a swap was refused.

Coins also flow the other way. The central float sends a coin down to a machine's hopper to keep it stocked, a machine hands a coin to a customer as change, and on a route visit the driver banks a coin of the day's takings back into the central float. The actions of the system are: a machine posting a deposit message and taking those coins out of its hopper, a compare-and-swap taking and adding the message's coins to the register, a compare-and-swap being refused and returning the message's coins to the machine's hopper, the float stocking a coin into a machine's hopper, a machine handing a coin to a customer, and the driver banking a coin of the takings back into the float.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The coins in the central register, plus the coins in each machine's hopper, plus the coins riding in each machine's posted deposit message, plus the coins already handed to customers always sum to exactly the number of coins the system started with.

CONSTANTS

    ArmTwo = sortArmTwo
    Bags = {bagA, bagB}
    NumChutes = 2
    NoBag = noBag

INVARIANT BagsArePartitioned
PROPERTY GrippersAlwaysOpenAgain
nl:
An airport baggage router feeds bags off a single input belt into a bank of numbered chutes. Two sorter arms work the belt. A shared cursor register says which chute is next in the rotation, and the arms coordinate on it by compare-and-swap rather than by locking, because the belt cannot be stopped.

An arm that is empty picks a bag off the belt into its gripper and, at that moment, notes the value the cursor register holds. The bag is now in the gripper and nowhere else -- it has left the belt and has not reached a chute. When the arm swings over to drop, it compares: if the cursor still holds the value the arm noted, the swap takes, the bag goes into the chute that the cursor names, and the cursor advances to the next chute in the rotation. If the cursor has moved on because the other arm dropped first, the swap is refused and the arm puts the bag back on the belt, empty-handed and ready to try again.

An arm can also die mid-swing. It stops with no fault code and no signal, and whatever bag is in its gripper stays clamped there. The router's supervisor eventually notices an arm that has gone quiet, opens its gripper, puts whatever was clamped in it back on the belt, and brings the arm back into service.

The property the ramp crew care about is that no bag is ever lost or duplicated. Every bag in the system is either riding the input belt, clamped in exactly one arm's gripper, or resting in exactly one chute -- never in two of those at once and never in none of them. The actions of the system are: an arm picking a bag off the belt and noting the cursor, an arm's swap taking so the bag goes into the cursor's chute and the cursor advances, an arm's swap being refused so the bag goes back on the belt, an arm dying mid-swing with a bag clamped, and the supervisor opening a dead arm's gripper, returning the bag to the belt and returning the arm to service.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The bags on the belt, the bags clamped in grippers and the bags resting in chutes partition the whole set of bags, with no bag in two of those places and no bag clamped by two arms at once.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: An arm that has a bag clamped in its gripper eventually has an empty gripper again, whether the swap takes, the swap is refused, or the supervisor opens it.

    MaxDuration = 2
    MaxRenewals = 1

SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT OnlyTheLiveLeaseholderRinses
nl:
The spot-free rinse manifold on a car-wash conveyor is a single piece of plant: one deionised-water line, one valve tree, and enough pressure for exactly one bay at a time. Bays get at it by taking a lease. A lease names one bay and carries a countdown; while the countdown is above zero that bay owns the manifold, and when the countdown reaches zero the valve tree closes itself whether or not the bay has finished, which is the whole reason the plant is run on leases rather than on a request queue.

A bay may only open its rinse arch while it holds a live lease. When the countdown ticks to zero the manifold shuts every arch on the line in the same motion, so no arch is left open past the end of its lease. Once the countdown is at zero the lease itself is torn down and the manifold is free for the next bay to take. A bay that is getting through its cars faster than expected can renew, which puts the countdown back up to the full duration, but the plant only allows a fixed number of renewals per lease so that one bay cannot sit on the manifold all shift.

The full duration of a lease is not a constant. The plant operator retunes it during the day: shorter when the queue is long and the wash packages are quick, longer in the evening when the ceramic-coat package is running and a bay genuinely needs the manifold for a while. Retuning takes effect for leases granted or renewed after the change; a lease already counting down keeps counting down from where it is.

The actions of the system are: granting the manifold lease to a bay for the current full duration, a leaseholder opening its rinse arch, a bay closing its rinse arch, the countdown ticking down and, on reaching zero, shutting every arch on the line, tearing down a lease whose countdown has reached zero, a leaseholder renewing its lease back to the full duration while renewals remain, and the plant operator retuning the full duration.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every bay with its rinse arch open is the bay that currently holds the manifold lease and that lease's countdown has not yet reached zero, so two arches are never open at once.

CONSTANTS

    Supervisor = opSuper
    JobOne = spoolJobOne

    Versions = 2
    MaxTtl = 2
    MaxSeizures = 1
    NoOp = noOp
    NoJob = noJob
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT StagedEditsRestOnTheLiveLease
PROPERTY LeasesAlwaysEnd
nl:
A print shop's job spooler lets operators edit the ticket attached to a queued job -- stock, sides, finishing, due time. To edit a ticket an operator takes a lease on that job. A lease names one operator and carries a countdown; leases are not renewed, so every lease runs out on its own. While an operator holds a live lease on a job it may stage an edit, which means noting the job ticket's current version number and holding the edited ticket ready to write.

Committing a staged edit writes the ticket and advances that job's version number. What must never happen is a staged edit that is still considered writable while resting on a version the job has already moved past, because writing it would silently undo whatever moved the version. The spooler therefore ties staging to the lease: when a lease's countdown reaches zero, the lease ends and any edit staged against that job under that lease is thrown away in the same motion. An operator whose stage was thrown away has to take a fresh lease and re-note the version.

The shift supervisor has an override. A supervisor can seize the lease on any job at any time -- a rush order, a press about to go idle -- taking ownership away from whoever held it and setting a fresh countdown. Seizing throws away whatever edit was staged against that job by the previous holder, for exactly the same reason expiry does. The shop limits how many seizures a shift may contain, so the override cannot be used to hold a job open indefinitely.

The actions of the system are: an operator taking a lease on an unleased job, a leaseholder staging an edit and noting the job's current version, a leaseholder committing its staged edit and advancing the job's version, a lease's countdown ticking down, a lease whose countdown has reached zero ending and discarding any edit staged under it, and the supervisor seizing a job's lease, discarding the previous holder's staged edit and setting a fresh countdown.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every staged edit belongs to the operator that currently holds a live lease on the job it is staged against and rests on exactly the version that job is currently on.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A job that is under lease eventually becomes unleased again, because leases are never renewed and every countdown runs out.

nl:
Changing the package on a car already moving down a car-wash conveyor touches three boxes at once: the arch controller that decides which passes run, the payment terminal that holds the charge, and the dryer that reserves blower time. A change that lands on some of them and not others produces a car that is charged for ceramic coat and gets a basic rinse, so the shop drives package changes through a two-phase commit run by the line controller.

A round begins with the controller asking every box to prepare. A box that agrees votes yes and, at that moment, notes the version its own settings are on -- that noted version is the basis of the change it has prepared. A box that cannot take the change votes no. Once every box has voted, the controller decides: commit if all three voted yes, abort otherwise, and either way it puts a decision message out for each box.

The decision messages go over the shop's field bus, which reorders them freely -- the dryer often hears before the arch controller, and there is no ordering guarantee at all. A box that receives a commit applies the change, advances its own version and goes back to having no vote outstanding. A box that receives an abort simply drops its prepared change and goes back to having no vote outstanding. The round is over when the last decision message has been received.

A box may also change its own settings locally, but only between rounds, and only while it has no vote outstanding. That restriction is the whole point: a box that has voted yes has a prepared change resting on a noted version, and if the box moved its own version underneath that prepared change, applying it later would quietly wipe out the local change.

The actions of the system are: the controller opening a round and clearing every box's vote, a box voting yes and noting its current version, a box voting no, the controller deciding to commit once every box has voted yes, the controller deciding to abort when some box voted no, a box receiving a commit and advancing its version, a box receiving an abort and dropping its prepared change, and a box making a local settings change between rounds.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every box that has voted yes has its prepared change resting on exactly the version that box is currently on, and no box can be sitting on a prepared change while the controller is between rounds.

CONSTANTS

    WorkerTwo = regWorkerTwo
    Sections = {secA, secB}
    Ceiling = 2
    NoSection = noSection
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT WriteChainIsUnbroken
PROPERTY AttemptsAlwaysClear
nl:
A university's registration back end has a pool of workers applying roster changes to course sections. There are no locks. A worker picks a section, reads the version number the section's roster is on, works out the change, and then tries to write. The write only lands if the section is still on the version the worker read; otherwise somebody else got there first and the worker re-reads and tries again.

Each section keeps two things the auditors care about: the version it is currently on, and the version that the change now in force was computed against. A section that has never been written is on version zero and has nothing in force. Every write that lands records the version it was computed against and moves the section to the next version, which means the recorded bases form an unbroken chain: the change in force on a section was always computed against the version immediately before the one the section is on now. A lost update would show up as a break in that chain -- a change in force whose recorded base is two or more versions back, meaning something in between was written and then silently overwritten.

Sections stop accepting writes once they reach the registrar's version ceiling for the term; a worker holding an attempt against a section that has hit the ceiling abandons the attempt rather than retrying forever.

Workers crash silently. A worker simply stops, and the attempt it was holding stops with it -- there is no rollback to do, because an attempt that never landed changed nothing. The scheduler notices workers that have gone quiet, clears whatever attempt they were holding and puts them back in the pool.

The actions of the system are: a worker beginning an attempt on a section and reading that section's current version, a worker landing an attempt whose read version still matches and advancing the section, a worker re-reading a section whose version has moved under it, a worker abandoning an attempt on a section that has hit the ceiling, a worker crashing silently, and the scheduler clearing a crashed worker's attempt and returning it to the pool.

SAFETY PROPERTY: On every section that has been written, the change in force was computed against the version immediately preceding the one the section is on, and no worker's outstanding attempt was read from a version ahead of the section's current one.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A worker holding an outstanding attempt eventually holds none, whether it lands, abandons, or is cleared after crashing.

CONSTANTS
    Controllers = {ilkA, ilkB}
    Trains = {trainA, trainB}
    MaxEpoch = 2
    NoCtl = noCtl
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT TripsAreOneShotAndAttributed
nl:
On a subway line the signalling system can drop a train's emergency brake trip. Dropping the trip is not something you undo from the control room: the train stops where it stops, a supervisor walks the tunnel, and the service pattern is rewritten for the rest of the day. So the interlocking is built so that a given train's trip can be dropped at most once, and only by the controller that genuinely held authority when the order was written.

Authority moves between interlocking controllers by numbered reconfiguration. Each reconfiguration advances the epoch and records, against that epoch number, which controller holds authority in it. The record for an epoch is written once, when the epoch begins, and the whole history of who held authority in which epoch is what the incident investigators read afterwards.

Dropping a trip is a two-step, one-shot affair. First the authority for the current epoch issues a trip ticket against a train, and the ticket is stamped with the epoch it was issued in. Then the ticket is spent: the trip is dropped and the order records which controller dropped it. A ticket can only be spent in the epoch it was stamped with -- a ticket left over from an earlier epoch is stale and is withdrawn rather than spent, and the train goes back to having no ticket at all. A ticket that has been spent is never reissued, which is what makes the drop a once-only act.

Controllers fail silently, with no alarm at the control room. A controller that has gone quiet cannot spend a ticket, so a ticket stamped in an epoch whose authority has gone quiet simply sits until reconfiguration makes it stale. Quiet controllers are eventually restored by the maintenance crew.

The actions of the system are: reconfiguring to a new epoch and recording which controller holds authority in it, the current authority issuing a trip ticket against a train stamped with the current epoch, spending a current-epoch ticket to drop the trip and recording the controller that did it, withdrawing a stale ticket stamped in an earlier epoch, a controller going quiet, and a quiet controller being restored.

SAFETY PROPERTY: A train has a trip recorded against it exactly when its ticket has been spent, and every recorded trip names the controller that held authority in the epoch that train's ticket was stamped with.

CONSTANTS

    StuTwo = stuTwo
    Slots = {benchA, benchB}
    Replicas = {hallA, hallB, hallC}
    NoSlot = noSlot
    NoStudent = noStudent

INVARIANT SeatedStudentsHoldTheirSlot
PROPERTY ProposalsAlwaysSettle
nl:
Lab sections at a university have individually numbered bench slots, and the registration service allocates them by quorum rather than by a central lock, because the service runs replicated across data halls. A student who wants a bench puts up a proposal naming the slot they want. Replicas then vote on proposals. A proposal is carried once a strict majority of replicas have voted for it.

The rule that keeps the allocation sound is a rule about replicas, not about students: a replica will vote for at most one proposal per bench slot, ever. Having voted for someone's proposal on bench four, that replica will never vote for anybody else's proposal on bench four, even if the first proposal is withdrawn. Since carrying a proposal needs a strict majority and any two strict majorities overlap, two different students can never both carry a proposal on the same bench.

Votes travel over the inter-hall link, which reorders freely: a replica's vote may arrive long after a later replica's, and the tally a proposal has at any moment is just the set of votes that have landed so far. Carrying a proposal writes the student into the slot's allocation and marks the student as seated. A proposal that cannot be carried -- because it does not have a majority and the slot it names has already been allocated to somebody else -- is withdrawn, which clears the proposal and the votes landed against it, though it does not un-spend the replicas' votes.

A seated student can give the bench up: the allocation is cleared, the student stops being seated, and the proposal goes away.

The actions of the system are: a student putting up a proposal for a bench slot, a replica voting for a proposal on a slot it has not yet voted on, a proposal that has a majority and names a free slot being carried and seating the student, a proposal that lacks a majority or names an already-allocated slot being withdrawn, and a seated student giving up their bench.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every seated student is the student written into the allocation of the slot their proposal names, and every seated student's proposal was carried on the votes of a strict majority of replicas.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A student who has put up a proposal eventually either becomes seated or has that proposal cleared.

CONSTANTS
    Techs = {techA, techB}
    Shelves = {shelfA, shelfB}
    MaxCap = 2
    NoTech = noTech
    NoShelf = noShelf
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT CoolerEntryIsExclusive
nl:
A hospital blood bank tracks its inventory in a walk-in cooler that only one technician may be inside at a time. It is not a rule about crowding -- the cooler's door interlock cuts the compressor while the door is open, and two overlapping entries would put the whole stock outside its temperature window. Entry is therefore governed by two locks taken in a fixed order: first the facility lock, which the whole bank shares and which only one technician can hold, and then the lock on the particular shelf the technician is going to work at. Nobody may take a shelf lock without already holding the facility lock.

A technician who holds both locks is inside the cooler and working at that shelf. While inside, the technician can add a unit to the shelf or issue a unit off it. Leaving releases the shelf lock and the facility lock together, and the technician is no longer inside.

Shelf capacity is not fixed. The pathologist retunes a shelf's capacity during the day as the platelet and plasma mix changes, and the retune takes effect immediately for anybody adding units afterwards. Capacity may be lowered as well as raised, but never below what a shelf is already holding, because there is nowhere to put displaced units and moving stock between shelves is a separate, audited process. Adding a unit is only allowed while the shelf is under its capacity as it stands at that moment.

The actions of the system are: a technician taking the facility lock, a technician holding the facility lock taking a free shelf's lock and entering the cooler at that shelf, a technician inside adding a unit to their shelf while it is under capacity, a technician inside issuing a unit off their shelf, a technician leaving the cooler and releasing both locks, and the pathologist retuning a shelf's capacity to any value not below what that shelf currently holds.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every technician inside the cooler is the holder of the facility lock and holds the lock on the shelf they are working at, so two technicians are never inside at once.

    OpTwo = washOpTwo
    Recipes = {pkgBasic, pkgCeramic}
    MaxRoster = 1
    MaxRev = 2
    NoRecipe = noRecipe
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT BoardEntriesAreBadgedAndSane
PROPERTY BoardEntriesAlwaysClear
nl:
The recipe records on a car-wash conveyor -- which chemicals a package uses, at what dilution, for how many seconds -- are edited from the shop floor by operators carrying badges. There is no lock on a recipe. An operator opens a change against a recipe, notes the revision the recipe was on when it opened the change, and writes only if the recipe is still on that revision; if the revision has moved, the operator re-reads and works from the new one.

Badges are tied to the shift roster, and the roster carries a number. Rotating the roster at shift change advances that number and, in the same motion, clears the work-in-progress board: every change that any operator had open is wiped, because the operators who opened them are walking out of the building. An operator's badge carries the roster number it was issued against, and only a badge issued against the roster number currently in force can open or write anything. An operator whose badge is behind the roster is stale and must be re-badged before touching a recipe again; re-badging is only possible while the operator is on the current roster.

Operators also just stop. A badge reader goes flat, a pager dies, and the operator's terminal simply stops responding with no notification -- the shop only finds out because the change they had open never lands. The floor supervisor clears the quiet operator's open change and brings them back on.

The thing the chemical safety auditor checks is that nothing on the board was opened by somebody who should not have been touching it: every change currently open belongs to an operator whose badge matches the roster number in force, and no open change was noted against a revision the recipe has not actually reached.

The actions of the system are: rotating the roster to a new number and clearing every open change, re-badging an operator against the roster number in force, a badged operator opening a change against a recipe and noting its revision, a badged operator writing a change whose noted revision still matches and advancing the recipe, a badged operator re-reading a recipe whose revision moved underneath its open change, a badged operator abandoning an open change against a recipe that has already reached its revision ceiling for the term, an operator going quiet without notice, and the supervisor clearing a quiet operator's open change and bringing them back on.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every change currently open belongs to an operator whose badge matches the roster number in force, and rests on a revision no later than the one its recipe is actually on.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: An operator with a change open eventually has no change open, whether it writes, is cleared at shift change, or is cleared by the supervisor after going quiet.

CONSTANTS
    Positions = {twrPosA, twrPosB}
    Runways = {rwy09L, rwy27R}
    Ceiling = 2
    Headroom = 1
    MaxSeq = 2
    MaxOverrides = 1
    NoRunway = noRunway
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT CeilingIsNeverBreached
nl:
A busy airport allocates departure slots on its runways from several controller positions at once. There is no lock on a runway. A controller opens a claim against a runway and notes the sequence number that runway's movement list was on when the claim was opened. Committing the claim only works if the list is still on that sequence number; otherwise another position got a movement in first, and the controller re-reads and works from the new number.

Every runway has a hard movement ceiling, set by the noise abatement agreement and the arrestor-bed inspection schedule. The ceiling is not a soft target: exceeding it is a reportable event, and no path through the tower's software may put more movements on a runway than the ceiling allows. Movements come off the list again when an aircraft actually rolls, which frees room under the ceiling.

The duty supervisor has an override for the cases the optimistic path handles badly -- a medevac, a fuel emergency, a diversion that has to go now. Using the override forces a movement onto a runway without waiting for a claim's sequence number to line up. What the override does not do is lift the ceiling: a forced movement still has to fit under it, because the ceiling is the one number the tower cannot argue with. The supervisor is allowed a limited number of overrides per shift, logged and reviewed afterwards.

A controller holding a claim against a runway that has reached its ceiling gives the claim up rather than spinning on it, and comes back when a movement has rolled. The same applies when the runway's movement list has run to the end of the shift's sequence book: there is no number left to commit against, so the claim is given up.

The actions of the system are: a controller opening a claim against a runway and noting its sequence number, a controller committing a claim whose noted sequence number still matches and adding a movement, a controller re-reading a runway whose sequence number has moved under its claim, a controller giving up a claim against a runway that has reached its ceiling or run out its sequence book, the duty supervisor forcing a movement onto a runway under the ceiling and consuming one of the shift's overrides, and an aircraft rolling so a movement leaves the list.

SAFETY PROPERTY: No runway ever carries more movements than its hard ceiling, and no controller's outstanding claim was noted against a sequence number ahead of the one its runway is actually on.

CONSTANTS
    Terminals = {schedTermA, schedTermB}
    Rooms = 3
    MaxGen = 2
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT BookingsFitTheStaffedCeiling
nl:
A hospital's operating-room scheduler is written around a single compare-and-swap register. The register holds the count of rooms currently booked together with a generation number, and every scheduler terminal that wants to book or cancel does the same thing: read the generation, work out the change, then swap. The swap only takes if the generation is still the one that was read; otherwise another terminal got in first and the attempt is dropped, to be started again from a fresh read.

How many rooms can be booked at once is not a property of the building. It is a property of who is on shift: an operating room without an anaesthetist and a scrub team is not a room, it is a cupboard with a table in it. The staffing office therefore sets the number of staffed rooms during the day as people clock on and off, and that number is the ceiling on booked rooms. The ceiling moves both ways, but the staffing office may never set it below the number of rooms already booked -- a booked room has a patient consented, premedicated and often already in the anaesthetic bay, and there is no mechanism in the scheduler to un-book somebody because a nurse went home. Lowering staffing therefore waits for cases to finish.

A booking attempt whose swap takes adds a booked room, but only if the booking would still be under the staffed ceiling at the moment the swap lands, which is what stops a stale attempt from booking into a ceiling that has come down since it was read. A cancellation attempt whose swap takes removes a booked room. Every swap that takes, in either direction, advances the generation.

The actions of the system are: a terminal starting an attempt and reading the generation, a booking swap taking and adding a booked room under the ceiling, a cancellation swap taking and removing a booked room, an attempt being dropped because the generation has moved since it was read, or because the register has run out its generation book for the day, or because there is nothing left for it to do -- a booking attempt with the ceiling already reached, or a cancellation attempt with nothing booked --, and the staffing office setting the number of staffed rooms to any value not below the number already booked.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of booked rooms never exceeds the number of staffed rooms, and no outstanding attempt was read against a generation ahead of the register's current one.

CONSTANTS
    BankOne = memberBankOne
    BankTwo = memberBankTwo
    MaxTerm = 2
    MaxOverrides = 1
    NoBank = noBank
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT OnlyTheCurrentLeaderPosts
PROPERTY PostingRunsAlwaysClose
nl:
The overnight interbank settlement batch is driven by one member bank at a time. The banks elect a batch leader, and the election stamps a term number on the winner. Only the bank that is both the current leader and has itself caught up to the current term number may post settlement legs into the batch; every other bank is either not the leader or is running on a term that has already been superseded, and in either case its postings would be junk that the clearing house cannot reconcile.

Leaders fail. When the batch leader falls over, the seat is empty, that bank is marked down, and whatever posting run it had open is stopped where it stands. A new election fills the seat and advances the term, up to the highest term the batch register can record for one night; a bank that is marked down cannot win an election until the operations desk brings it back up. Banks that are not the leader learn about term advances lazily off the settlement bus, which is why a bank can be sitting on a stale term without knowing it.

The central bank's duty officer has an override. On a night when the elections are thrashing and the window is closing, the duty officer installs a leader directly: the named bank takes the seat, the term advances, that bank is brought level with the new term, and every posting run in progress anywhere is stopped. The override is rationed -- a fixed number per night, each one written into the morning report.

The actions of the system are: electing a leader for the batch and advancing the term, the leader failing and leaving the seat empty with its posting run stopped, a non-leader bank learning the current term off the settlement bus, the current leader opening a posting run, a bank closing its posting run, the duty officer installing a leader directly and stopping every posting run, and the operations desk bringing a downed bank back up.

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every bank with a posting run open holds the batch leader's seat and has caught up to the current term number.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A bank that has a posting run open eventually has no posting run open.

nl:
A container terminal moves boxes between three places: the ship's cells, the quay stack alongside the crane, and the yard block inland. A box is always in exactly one of those three places -- the terminal's whole accounting rests on it, because a box that is on the books in two places is a box that will be looked for in the wrong one, and a box on the books in none of them is a box that has been lost.

No single planner may order a move. The terminal runs three planning systems -- the stowage planner, the yard planner and the crane scheduler -- and a move only goes ahead once a strict majority of them have approved that particular box's move. Approvals accumulate against the box: a planner adds its approval, and when the majority is there the move is executed and the box's approvals are cleared, because the next move has to be approved on its own merits. Approvals can also be cleared without a move, which is what happens when the planning cycle rolls over and the planners re-plan from the berth schedule.

The moves themselves are the ordinary sequence of a discharge and a re-stow: a box comes off the ship onto the quay stack, a box goes from the quay stack into the yard block, and a box comes back out of the yard block onto the quay stack for a later loading.

The terminal superintendent has an override. When the crane is about to go idle and the planners have not converged, the superintendent forces a box off the quay stack into the yard block without waiting for a majority. The override is rationed and each use is logged; what it does not do is invent or destroy a box, because the box still goes from exactly one place to exactly one other.

The actions of the system are: a planner approving a box's move, a box moving from the ship to the quay stack on a majority, a box moving from the quay stack to the yard block on a majority, a box moving from the yard block back to the quay stack on a majority, the superintendent forcing a box from the quay stack to the yard block without a majority, and the planners clearing a box's accumulated approvals at a planning cycle rollover.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The boxes on the ship, the boxes on the quay stack and the boxes in the yard block partition the whole set of boxes, so no box is ever in two of those places and none is in fewer than one.

nl:
An approach control facility hands landing clearances out of a shared pool. The pool has a hard size: the number of aircraft that may be inside the final approach corridor at once, fixed by the separation minima and the runway occupancy time. Each approach sector takes a lease when it wants to run an aircraft down the corridor, and a lease occupies one place in the pool for as long as it is live. The facility also works to a fixed issue budget: only so many leases may be granted in one watch, after which the corridor is closed out and the next watch starts a fresh book.

Every lease carries a countdown, wound to the full lease duration when it is granted. The countdown runs down step by step. When it reaches its last step the lease expires: the lease is torn down and its place in the pool is handed back in the same motion. A sector that has finished early can also give its lease back before the countdown runs out, which frees the place immediately. What must never happen is a lease that is live with no countdown left on it, because that is a place in the pool that nothing will ever hand back.

Sectors fail silently. A sector position can lose its data feed and stop working the corridor without any indication to the facility -- no alarm, no handover, and no early release of the lease it is holding. This is exactly the case the lease countdown exists for: the failed sector's place comes back when the lease expires, whether or not anybody at that position is still alive to notice. A silently failed sector is eventually brought back onto the position by the watch supervisor.

Because places only leave the pool when a lease is granted and only return when a lease is torn down or given back, the number of live leases never exceeds the size of the pool, and the corridor never holds more aircraft than the separation minima allow.

The actions of the system are: granting a sector a lease while the pool has a free place and the watch's issue budget has not run out, a live lease's countdown running down one step, a lease expiring on its last step and handing its place back, a sector giving its lease back early, a sector failing silently, and the watch supervisor bringing a failed sector back onto position.

SAFETY PROPERTY: The number of live leases never exceeds the size of the clearance pool, and no live lease has a countdown of zero left on it.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: A sector that holds a live lease eventually holds none, because every countdown runs out even when the sector has silently failed.

CONSTANTS NumSlots, NumDevices, NumNorthDevices, MaxEpoch

HubOf(d) == IF d <= NumNorthDevices THEN "north" ELSE "south"

vars == <<pool, installer, credential, lease, epoch, waiting>>

  /\ pool \in [Slots -> {"north", "south", "free"}]
  /\ installer \in [Slots -> {"north", "south", "free"}]
  /\ credential \in [Slots -> Devices \cup {0}]
  /\ lease \in [Slots -> 0..MaxEpoch]
  /\ epoch \in 0..MaxEpoch
  /\ waiting \subseteq Devices

CredentialsMatchSlotLease ==
  \A s \in Slots :
    credential[s] # 0 => installer[s] = pool[s]

Init ==
  /\ pool = [s \in Slots |-> "free"]
  /\ installer = [s \in Slots |-> "free"]
  /\ credential = [s \in Slots |-> 0]
  /\ lease = [s \in Slots |-> 0]
  /\ epoch = 0
  /\ waiting = {}

Enroll(d) ==
  /\ d \notin waiting
  /\ \A s \in Slots : credential[s] # d
  /\ waiting' = waiting \cup {d}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, installer, credential, lease, epoch>>

AcquireLease(h, s) ==
  /\ pool[s] = "free"
  /\ pool' = [pool EXCEPT ![s] = h]
  /\ lease' = [lease EXCEPT ![s] = epoch]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<installer, credential, epoch, waiting>>

ProgramSlot(h, d, s) ==
  /\ pool[s] = h
  /\ HubOf(d) = h
  /\ d \in waiting
  /\ credential[s] = 0
  /\ lease[s] = epoch
  /\ credential' = [credential EXCEPT ![s] = d]
  /\ installer' = [installer EXCEPT ![s] = h]
  /\ waiting' = waiting \ {d}
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, lease, epoch>>

Rekey ==
  /\ epoch < MaxEpoch
  /\ epoch' = epoch + 1
  /\ UNCHANGED <<pool, installer, credential, lease, waiting>>

ReleaseLease(h, s) ==
  /\ pool[s] = h
  /\ pool' = [pool EXCEPT ![s] = "free"]
  /\ lease' = [lease EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
  /\ credential' = [credential EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
  /\ installer' = [installer EXCEPT ![s] = "free"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, waiting>>

SeizeStaleSlot(h, s) ==
  /\ pool[s] # "free"
  /\ pool[s] # h
  /\ lease[s] < epoch
  /\ pool' = [pool EXCEPT ![s] = h]
  /\ lease' = [lease EXCEPT ![s] = epoch]
  /\ credential' = [credential EXCEPT ![s] = 0]
  /\ installer' = [installer EXCEPT ![s] = "free"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<epoch, waiting>>

Next ==
  \/ \E d \in Devices : Enroll(d)
  \/ \E h \in {"north", "south"}, s \in Slots : AcquireLease(h, s)
  \/ \E h \in {"north", "south"}, d \in Devices, s \in Slots : ProgramSlot(h, d, s)
  \/ Rekey
  \/ \E h \in {"north", "south"}, s \in Slots : ReleaseLease(h, s)
  \/ \E h \in {"north", "south"}, s \in Slots : SeizeStaleSlot(h, s)

    NumNorthDevices = 1

nl:
A smart-home vendor sells two hub products that customers routinely install in the same house: a north-side hub that manages the front door and porch locks, and a south-side hub that manages the garage and patio locks. The two hubs were written by different teams and never talk to each other, but they both drive the same physical lock controller, which exposes one shared pool of credential slots. A slot can hold at most one programmed device credential at a time, and the lock controller itself has no idea which hub asked for what -- it simply records, alongside each credential, which hub wrote it.

Access to the pool is arbitrated by leases stamped with a network-wide configuration epoch. Taking a lease on a free slot is a separate step from programming a credential into it: a hub first acquires the lease, and only afterwards, and only while its lease is still stamped with the current epoch, does it write one of its own enrolled devices into the slot. That gap matters, because a leased-but-unprogrammed slot is a perfectly normal state that the installer sees all the time.

Devices are enrolled onto a waiting list when the homeowner adds them, and leave the waiting list when a hub programs them into a slot. A hub can release its own lease at any point, which hands the slot back to the pool; releasing has to wipe the credential off the lock and clear the recorded installer, because the slot is about to become available to the other hub.

Reconfiguration is where the two hubs collide. Whenever the household layout changes, the epoch is bumped once, network-wide. A lease still stamped with an older epoch is stale: it was taken under a layout that no longer applies. A hub is entitled to seize such a stale slot away from the other hub without any handshake, re-stamping the lease with the current epoch. Seizing must also wipe whatever the previous hub had programmed there and clear the recorded installer, since the new lessee has not written anything yet.

The failure mode this model exists to rule out is a slot on the shared lock that still carries one hub's credential while the lease has moved to the other hub -- a garage remote that still opens the front door, or a retired badge that the current lessee never wrote and cannot account for. Both the release path and the seize path have to tear down the credential and the lease together, or the same slot ends up effectively allocated twice.

The actions in this model are: Enroll (a device joins the waiting list), AcquireLease (a hub takes a lease on a free slot, stamping it with the current epoch), ProgramSlot (a hub with a current-epoch lease writes one of its own waiting devices into the slot and records itself as the installer), Rekey (the network-wide epoch is bumped once), ReleaseLease (a hub gives up its own lease, wiping the credential and the recorded installer), and SeizeStaleSlot (a hub takes over a slot whose lease predates the current epoch, wiping the previous hub's credential and installer).

SAFETY PROPERTY: Whenever a slot on the shared lock carries a programmed credential, the hub recorded as having installed that credential is exactly the hub that currently holds the slot's lease.

vars == <<token, version, stock, base, phase>>

  /\ version \in 0..MaxVersion
  /\ stock \in 0..InitialStock
  /\ base \in [Stations -> 0..MaxVersion]
  /\ phase \in [Stations -> {"idle", "reading", "staged"}]

  \A st \in Stations :
    phase[st] # "idle" =>
      /\ token = st
      /\ base[st] = version

Init ==
  /\ token = 1
  /\ version = 0
  /\ stock = InitialStock
  /\ base = [st \in Stations |-> 0]
  /\ phase = [st \in Stations |-> "idle"]

PassToken ==
  /\ phase[token] = "idle"
  /\ token' = NextInRing(token)
  /\ UNCHANGED <<version, stock, base, phase>>

BeginRead(st) ==
  /\ token = st
  /\ phase[st] = "idle"
  /\ base' = [base EXCEPT ![st] = version]
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![st] = "reading"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, version, stock>>

StageDeduction(st) ==
  /\ token = st
  /\ phase[st] = "reading"
  /\ stock > 0
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![st] = "staged"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, version, stock, base>>

Commit(st) ==
  /\ token = st
  /\ phase[st] = "staged"
  /\ stock > 0
  /\ version < MaxVersion
  /\ version' = version + 1
  /\ stock' = stock - 1
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![st] = "idle"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, base>>

Abandon(st) ==
  /\ phase[st] # "idle"
  /\ phase' = [phase EXCEPT ![st] = "idle"]
  /\ UNCHANGED <<token, version, stock, base>>

  \/ PassToken
  \/ \E st \in Stations : BeginRead(st)
  \/ \E st \in Stations : StageDeduction(st)
  \/ \E st \in Stations : Commit(st)
  \/ \E st \in Stations : Abandon(st)

CONSTANTS
    NumStations = 2
    MaxVersion = 2
    InitialStock = 2
SPECIFICATION Spec
INVARIANT InFlightWritesSeeCurrentVersion
nl:
A hospital pharmacy runs several dispensing stations along a single automated cabinet. Each station is a workstation where a pharmacist pulls a prescription, checks it, and deducts the dispensed units from one shared inventory record. The record has two fields that matter here: the number of units still in the cabinet, and a version counter that is bumped once for every deduction that lands.

The stations coordinate with a token that circulates around a fixed ring. Only the station currently holding the token is allowed to open a dispensing transaction against the shared record, and the token can only be handed to the next station in the ring when the current holder has nothing in flight. There is no timeout and no way to yank the token back: a pharmacist can be interrupted by a phone call and sit on the token for a long time, but the system never assumes a station has died and never re-issues the token behind its back. Slow is tolerated; failed is out of scope.

A dispensing transaction is deliberately multi-step, because that is where the danger lives. The holder first reads the shared record, recording the version it saw as the base for its update. Then it stages the deduction, having confirmed there is stock to take. Only afterwards does it commit, which decrements the stock and bumps the version. A pharmacist who is interrupted mid-transaction can abandon it at any point before or after staging, which throws the work away and returns the station to idle without touching the shared record.

The failure this model is built to catch is the classic lost update: a station reads the record, some other station commits a deduction in the meantime, and then the first station commits anyway on top of the stale read, silently erasing the other deduction. The units come off the shelf twice but the record only remembers once, and the cabinet count drifts away from physical stock. The ring is what is supposed to prevent that, by ensuring the read and the commit of a single transaction are never separated by anyone else's commit.

The actions in this model are: PassToken (the idle holder hands the token to the next station in the ring), BeginRead (the token holder opens a transaction and records the version it read), StageDeduction (the token holder confirms stock and stages the deduction), Commit (the token holder applies the deduction, decrementing stock and bumping the version), and Abandon (a station throws away an in-flight transaction and returns to idle).

SAFETY PROPERTY: Any station with a transaction in flight is the current token holder, and the version it read when it opened that transaction is still the version of the shared record.

PROPERTY EveryTaskingEventuallyLands
nl:
A wildfire agency flies a surveillance drone swarm over an active burn. Two tasking services decide where the drones look: a fire-line planner that tracks the advancing head of the fire, and a perimeter planner that watches the containment edge. The two services were procured separately, run on separate ground stations, and share exactly one thing -- the sector tasking record that the drones actually read. That record is kept as an append-only journal: every accepted tasking update is appended as an entry naming the planner that wrote it and the journal length it was computed from.

There is no lock on the record. Both services use optimistic concurrency. A planner reads the current journal length as the base for its update, spends time computing a plan against that snapshot, and then attempts to append. The append is accepted only if the journal has not grown since the read; if it has, the planner's plan was computed against a record that no longer exists and the append is refused, so the planner throws the plan away and starts over. A planner that has been refused once stops trusting the fast path and switches permanently to the careful staged path for the rest of the incident.

The fast path is the shorthand both services ship by default: read the journal length and append in one indivisible step, which cannot be raced. The careful path splits the work into a read, a planning interval, and a separate commit attempt, which is exactly where another service's append can slip in between.

The hazard is the lost update. If a planner is allowed to append a plan that was computed from an older journal, the tasking the other service just published is silently superseded by a plan that never saw it, and a sector everybody believes is being watched is watched by nobody. The journal is supposed to record a strict chain: the first entry was computed from an empty record, the second from a record holding exactly the first entry, and so on with no gaps and no rewrites.

Each service has exactly one sector tasking to publish for this incident, and neither is finished until its tasking is actually in the shared journal. Refusals are expected and are not failures, but a service must not be starved by the other one forever.

The actions in this model are: StartRead (a pending planner reads the current journal length as its base and begins planning), FinishPlan (a planner finishes computing and becomes ready to commit), CommitPlan (a ready planner appends its entry, but only if the journal has not grown since its read), RetryPlan (a ready planner whose base is stale discards its plan and switches to the careful mode), FastPath (a planner still in optimistic mode reads and appends in one indivisible step), and Standby (once no service has a tasking left to publish, the incident model idles in place).

SAFETY PROPERTY: Every entry in the shared tasking journal was computed from the journal state that immediately precedes it, so the i-th entry always records a base of i minus one.

LIVENESS PROPERTY: Every planner that still has a tasking to publish eventually has an entry of its own in the shared journal.
